gotcha-langs.race_n.py:
import sys
import threading

N, THREADS = int(sys.argv[1]), 8
total = 0  # shared by every thread


def term(i):
    return i


def add(lo, hi):
    global total
    for i in range(lo, hi):
        total = total + term(i)  # read total, call a function, write total


step = N // THREADS
threads = [threading.Thread(target=add, args=(p * step + 1, (p + 1) * step + 1)) for p in range(THREADS)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print("exact" if total == N * (N + 1) // 2 else "lost", end=" ")

gotcha.title: Sharing a counter between parallel closures
gotcha.looks_fine: Adding every number into one shared variable from several workers is a short, natural way to total a list.
gotcha.rust_sees: `for_each` calls your closure from several threads at once, so the closure has to be `Sync` and `Send`. This one borrows an `Rc<RefCell<u64>>`, and the error says `Sync` is not implemented for it: `Rc` counts its owners without atomics, and `RefCell` checks borrows without any locking.
gotcha.why: The compiler is refusing a data race before it can happen. This is the check from [Send and Sync](/learn/send-sync/) applied to rayon's closures. The fix is usually to stop sharing: let each piece return a value and let rayon combine them (`sum`, `reduce`). If you do need shared state, use an atomic or an `Arc<Mutex<T>>` ([Shared State](/learn/shared-state/)).

fixed.name: src/main.rs

go.says: Go compiles and runs this. One goroutine per CPU (eight on this VM) adds into one `int` with no lock, and `total += i` is a read, an add and a write, so updates get lost. The run printed a total below the expected one, and `go run -race` reports a data race in this program.

java.says: Java compiles and runs this. A parallel stream calls the lambda on several threads, and `total[0] += n` is a read, an add and a write, so updates get lost. The run printed a total below the expected one.

kotlin.says: This uses the same Java stream as the Java version and fails the same way (`kotlinx.coroutines` was not run). The run printed a total below the expected one.

csharp.says: C# compiles and runs this. `Parallel.For` runs the body on several threads and `total += n` is not atomic (`Interlocked.Add` exists for this). The run printed a total below the expected one.

c.says: gcc compiles this with `-fopenmp`. Every thread updates `total`. Two sources apply, and they say different things. The OpenMP 5.2 memory model ([section 1.4.1](https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.2/openmpsu9.html)) says "If a data race occurs then the result of the program is unspecified". The C11 standard (section 5.1.2.4), for threads as the C standard defines them, says a data race is undefined behavior. Either way nothing promises the result. The run printed a total below the expected one. A `reduction(+ : total)` clause is the fix, as in the table below.

cpp.says: g++ compiles this with `-fopenmp`. Every thread updates `total`. Two sources apply, and they say different things. The OpenMP 5.2 memory model ([section 1.4.1](https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.2/openmpsu9.html)) says "If a data race occurs then the result of the program is unspecified". The C++ standard ([intro.races](https://eel.is/c++draft/intro.races)) says a data race is undefined behavior, for the threads it defines. Either way nothing promises the result. The run printed a total below the expected one.

python.says: Python runs this. The global interpreter lock keeps the interpreter's own data consistent, but `total = total + term(i)` is still a read, a call and a write, so updates get lost. Whether it loses updates depends on how long each thread runs before the interpreter switches threads, so it depends on the size: the session under the gotcha runs this loop five times at each of three sizes. This tab uses 8,000,000 numbers, and its run printed a total below the expected one. Not guaranteed either way ([Shared State](/learn/shared-state/) has the details).

typescript.says: Node runs this, and there is no race and no sum either. Each worker thread gets its own copy of `total`, so the main thread printed 0. Workers can share memory by sharing a `SharedArrayBuffer` or by transferring an `ArrayBuffer`, as the [Node docs](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/worker_threads.html) say. A plain variable like `total` is not shared.
